metaData.originalTitle: Lines of Code Got a Better Publicist
metaData.title: Lines of Code Got a Better Publicist
metaData.oneSentenceSummary: This article argues that the industry's shift from outcome-based productivity metrics to volume-based AI adoption claims (e.g., '% of code written by AI') is a regression to vanity metrics, and urges a return to measuring what matters.
metaData.summary: The author, a veteran software engineer, draws a parallel between the old, discredited practice of measuring developer productivity by lines of code and the current trend of AI vendors touting volume-based metrics like '75% of new code is AI-generated.' He contrasts these with earlier, more meaningful outcome claims like GitHub's '55% faster task completion.' The article reviews the complex and often contradictory research on AI's productivity impact, including studies showing gains for juniors, increased code churn, and even slower performance for experienced devs in their own codebases. It critiques the rise of 'AI Adoption Maturity Models' as another form of measuring adoption intensity rather than actual value. The author's core concern is that these vanity metrics are being used to justify major business decisions, such as the large-scale layoffs at Block and Atlassian, where AI is cited as the reason for needing fewer people. He argues that if AI truly made everyone more productive, companies would use that capacity to deliver more value, not cut headcount. The article concludes by advocating for an 'AI-first' approach to work but a 'battle-tested' approach to measurement, urging readers to always ask: 'Is that an outcome, or a volume?'

mainPoints.point: Volume-based AI metrics like '% of code written by AI' are the new 'lines of code' vanity metric.
mainPoints.explanation: The author argues that these claims, popularized by AI vendors, measure adoption intensity, not actual business value or developer effectiveness, mirroring the discredited practice of counting lines of code.

mainPoints.point: The research on AI's productivity impact is complex and contradictory, not a simple success story.
mainPoints.explanation: While some studies show significant speedups (e.g., +26% tasks for juniors), others show increased code churn, decreased refactoring, and even slower performance for experienced developers in familiar codebases. The evidence does not support a simple 'AI makes everyone faster' narrative.

mainPoints.point: Using AI adoption metrics to justify layoffs is a flawed and potentially disingenuous argument.
mainPoints.explanation: The author points to layoffs at Block and Atlassian, arguing that if AI truly created a massive productivity gain, the logical outcome would be to deliver more value, not reduce headcount. This suggests the productivity claim is a post-hoc justification for other business decisions.

mainPoints.point: Engineers should adopt AI tools, but measure their impact using established, outcome-based metrics.
mainPoints.explanation: The author advocates for an 'AI-first' approach to work but insists on using 'battle-tested' metrics like DORA, reliability, and customer value to measure success, rather than falling for new, unproven vanity metrics.

keyQuotes: "Percent of code written by AI" is just lines of code with a better publicist.
The 2026 claims can't fail. That's the genius of them; "75% of our code is AI-written" could be true, and will keep going up, regardless of whether anything got better.
When a company says "AI made everyone more productive, so we need fewer people", I want to see the evidence - and I don't believe it exists today.
Adoption is the *starting line*, not the scoreboard.
Be AI-first in how you work, but battle-tested in how you measure it.

relatedArticles.title: Introducing Claude Opus 4.7
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Anthropic has released Claude Opus 4.7, a significant upgrade over Opus 4.6 with major improvements in advanced software engineering, vision capabilities, instruction following, and autonomous long-horizon reasoning, while implementing new cyber safeguards and maintaining the same pricing.

relatedArticles.title: Cursor and SpaceX Partner to Scale AI Coding with Stargate-Class Infrastructure
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Cursor CEO Michael Truell announces a strategic partnership with SpaceX to leverage massive compute infrastructure for scaling the Cursor Composer and building advanced coding models.

relatedArticles.title: Software Architecture Guide
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This page from Martin Fowler presents his perspective on software architecture, defining it as the important stuff in system design, and serves as a curated guide to his site's extensive resources on application and enterprise architecture.

relatedArticles.title: Andrej Karpathy on Code Agents， AutoResearch， and the Loopy Era of AI
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Andrej Karpathy explores the paradigm shift from manual programming to agent orchestration, the automation of AI research, and the profound implications for software engineering and education.

relatedArticles.title: Harness design for long-running application development
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article explores Anthropic's multi-agent harness design (Planner, Generator, Evaluator) for long-running autonomous coding, detailing how to overcome context anxiety and self-evaluation bias to build complex full-stack applications.

relatedArticles.title: Martin Fowler & Kent Beck: Frameworks for reinventing software， again and again
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Software legends Martin Fowler and Kent Beck discuss how AI redefines software engineering, emphasizing that core practices like TDD and modularity remain essential for human-AI collaboration.

relatedArticles.title: Dario Amodei — Policy on the AI Exponential
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Dario Amodei argues that AI is advancing exponentially, creating a dangerous mismatch with slow-moving policy, and proposes concrete actions across regulation, economics, science, civil liberties, and geopolitics to meet the moment.

relatedArticles.title: Inside FAISS: Billion-Scale Similarity Search
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: This article provides a deep, visual, and intuitive explanation of FAISS, covering the core ideas of IVF, Product Quantization, their combination in IVFPQ, and GPU acceleration, to enable billion-scale similarity search.

relatedArticles.title: Harness engineering: leveraging Codex in an agent-first world
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: OpenAI engineers detail a five-month experiment building a production software product with zero manually-written code, using Codex agents to achieve 10x velocity and redefining the engineer's role as system designer and feedback loop architect.

relatedArticles.title: Xiaomi MiMo， Explore and Love
relatedArticles.oneSentenceSummary: Xiaomi MiMo and TileRT achieve 1000+ tokens/s inference on a 1-trillion-parameter model using commodity GPUs through extreme model-system codesign, including FP4 quantization and DFlash speculative decoding.
